catalog_citation: Jones, Michael (1988). Sardinian. In M. Harris & N. Vincent (eds.), The Romance Languages, 314-350. London: Croom Helm [description based on Logudorese-Nuorese, sample dialect Lula (Nuorese); read via archive.org scanned text of the page scan]. Screen source also…
catalog_locator: Jones 1988, sec. 2 Phonology, 'Syllable Structure and Word-stress', pp. 326-327 (stress paragraph p. 327); orthographic convention p. 316; verb paradigms p. 333
catalog_quote: Word-stress normally falls on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. Stress on final syllables is generally avoided in Sardinian. Indeed, a final epenthetic vowel is added to Latin monosyllables to yield paroxytonic forms. ... However, oxytonic forms do arise, mainly in Campidanese and Logudorese, as a result of elision of an intervocalic consonant: Log. /'pe/ (< pedem) 'foot', Camp. /dro'mi/ (< dOrmIre) 'to sleep'. A further process which yields final stress is truncation of the post-tonic sequence in vocative uses of nouns (particularly proper names and diminutives) and certain imperatives: /ju'a/ (<- /ju'anne/ 'John'), /pitsin'ne/ (<- /pitsin'neddu, -a/ 'little boy/ girl'), /a'ba/ (<- /a'barra/ 'stay'), /'te/ (<- /'tene/ 'hold'). When a verb (e.g. an imperative) is followed by a single clitic, the verb retains its normal stress pattern. However, if two or more clitics are added…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and all auxiliary snippets (pp. 316, 326-327, 333) are present verbatim at the stated places in the held archive.org scanned text of Jones 1988; the second reader's independent confirmation stands. (2) Deciding source: a 1988 handbook grammar sketch by a Sardinian specialist, explicitly describing Logudorese-Nuorese (Lula), so languoid identity is correct; it is reputable but not the fullest or most recent phonological description (Molinu 2017, Contini 1987, Pittau 1972, Corda 1994, Mensching & Remberger 2016 exist; none held, none open). (3) Open sources fetched sources now — Lai 2002 (instrumental thesis on Nuoro prosody, HAL), Molinu 2021 (HDR synthesis, HAL), Vanrell et al. 2014 (Loquens, OA), Hofmann 1885 (archive.org) — all either confirm or are silent: stress type is a lexical property within the last three syllables, paroxytones dominate (Lai's lexicon counts)

sources.citation: Molinu, Lucia (2021). Contraintes et variation en sarde et ailleurs. Mémoire de synthèse pour l'Habilitation à diriger des recherches, Université Toulouse Jean Jaurès. 137 pp. HAL tel-03348417.
sources.quote: Synthesis of Molinu's work on (mainly Logudorese, Buddusò) Sardinian phonology. States a constraint against oxytony in Sardinian, repaired by vowel epenthesis (ki > kie, mi > mie, tu > tue; fn. 38), a disyllabic-trochee minimal word, and that truncated monosyllabic imperatives (mi' < mira, na' < nara, te' < tene) and truncated vocatives ([an'tɔ] < [an'tɔna]) are oxytone forms at the periphery of the system that escape repair. No general stress-placement algorithm is given; stress position is treated as lexical (proparoxytone vs paroxytone verb types discussed pp. 80-82).

sources.citation: Vanrell, Maria del Mar; Ballone, Francesc; Schirru, Carlo; Prieto, Pilar (2014). Intonation and its interfaces in Sardinian polar questions. Loquens 1(2), e014. doi:10.3989/loquens.2014.014 (open access).
sources.quote: Logudorese/Nuorese and Campidanese speakers. 'Considering that the vast majority of Sardinian words are paroxytones (Vanrell et al., in press), many scholars have found it most practical to write a graphic accent only on words with final and antepenultimate stress, and this is the criterion followed here.' Cites Jones 1988 for segmental deletions. Intonation study; no stress algorithm.

sources.citation: Lai, Jean-Pierre (2002). L'intonation du parler de Nuoro (Sardaigne). Thèse de doctorat, Université Stendhal Grenoble 3. 321 pp. HAL tel-01237122.
sources.quote: Instrumental intonation thesis on Nuorese. Treats accent type as a lexical property of each word and counts them in a Nuoro dictionary sample (table A, p. 52): trisyllables 31% paroxytone vs 7.5% proparoxytone vs 0.03% oxytone; quadrisyllables 28% parox. vs 4% proparox.; oxytone monosyllables 0.1%; one marginal 'pré-proparoxyton' class (0.03%, six-syllable words). p. 23: a fixed paragogic [e] is added after final stressed vowels ([ki]->[kie], [tu]->[tue], caffè -> [kaffe]) 'par l'hostilité des sardes à l'égard de l'oxytonie'; fn. 234 p. 85: 'M. L. Wagner (1984 [1941], § 13) avait déjà fait rem
sources.locator: ch. I sec. 1.10.1 p. 23 (paragoge after oxytones); ch. II table A p. 52 (accent-type counts over a 3300-word Nuoro lexicon sample); ch. III p. 84-85 with fn. 234

sources.citation: Hofmann, Gustav (1885). Die logudoresische und campidanesische Mundart. Marburg: R. Friedrich (Strassburg dissertation). 168 pp. archive.org bub_gb_hhxDAQAAMAAJ (scanned text).
sources.quote: Historical Lautlehre (Glottolog hhtype phonology). The only stress section lists where verb stress deviates from Latin: 2nd-conj. infinitives retract stress to the stem (ténnere, párrere), 1/2pl present of Latin 3rd conj. stress the penultimate (leghímus), some Latin proparoxytone presents become paroxytone (consíderas), Logudorese 1/2pl imperfect subjunctive shifts stress one syllable forward (timerémus). No synchronic word-stress rule; consistent with lexically/morphologically specified stress.
